summary: Describes how to authenticate IS-IS packets using HMAC-MD5, so routers can check that routing messages come from trusted neighbors. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 5304.

eli5.summary: Routers pass notes to each other about the best roads. This memo adds a secret signature to each note, so a router can tell a fake note from a real one.

questions: how does is-is hmac-md5 authentication work
does is-is authentication stop replay attacks
subtitle: How IS-IS routers can sign their routing messages with HMAC-MD5 so that forged ones are rejected.

tldr.problem: The base IS-IS specification only defines cleartext passwords, which do not stop an attacker from injecting false routing information.
tldr.mechanism: A new authentication type, 54, carries a 16-byte HMAC-MD5 value computed over the PDU, with rules for which fields are zeroed and which key is used per PDU type.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo has been obsoleted by RFC 5304, so it no longer describes the current method.

today: RFC 3567 is an Informational memo that has been obsoleted by RFC 5304, so that is the document to read for IS-IS cryptographic authentication.

sections.title: Authentication in IS-IS
sections.content:
IS-IS, specified in ISO 10589 with IPv4 extensions in RFC 1195, can authenticate its Link State PDUs by including an authentication TLV. That TLV has type 10 and a variable length. The first octet of its value is the authentication type: 0 is reserved, 1 is a cleartext password, and 255 is for routing domain private methods. The rest is the Authentication Value.

RFC 3567 adds a new authentication type for HMAC-MD5 (defined in RFC 2104) and specifies how to compute the value. It also changes some base protocol behaviour so the mechanism is effective. It comes from the IS-IS Working Group and is a contribution to ISO for eventual inclusion in ISO 10589.
sections.eli5: IS-IS routers already had a spot for a password on each message, but only a plain, readable one. This memo adds a better, secret kind of stamp.

sections.title: Computing and Checking the HMAC-MD5 Value
sections.content:
The authentication type for HMAC-MD5 is 54 (0x36). The Authentication Value is 16 bytes long, so the TLV length field is 17. The key K is the password for the PDU type, and the text T is the whole PDU with the Authentication Value set to zero (and the type and length already set to 54 and 17). For LSPs the Checksum and Remaining Lifetime fields are also zeroed before computing. The result goes into the Authentication Value field.

Which password is used depends on the PDU. Level 1 Sequence Number PDUs use the Area Authentication string, Level 2 ones use the domain authentication string, and IS-IS HELLO PDUs use the Link Level Authentication String, which MAY differ from the LSP one. HELLO results are computed after padding to the MTU size, if padding is not disabled. Implementations MUST NOT include the Checksum TLV in these PDUs.

To check an incoming PDU, save the Authentication Value, Checksum and Remaining Lifetime, zero them, compute, and restore them. An implementation that supports HMAC-MD5 MUST discard a PDU whose value is wrong.
sections.eli5: The sender mixes the message with a shared secret to make a short stamp. The receiver does the same mix and throws the message away if the stamps do not match.

sections.title: Transition, Rollover and Purges
sections.content:
An implementation MAY have a transition mode that adds the HMAC-MD5 information but does not verify it, as an aid while authentication is being deployed. It MAY also check a set of passwords, which allows passwords to be changed step by step. One that does not implement HMAC-MD5 MAY accept a PDU containing this type.

Purges need special care. A system that implements HMAC-MD5 and starts an LSP purge MUST remove the body of the LSP and add the authentication TLV. It MUST NOT accept unauthenticated purges, nor purges with TLVs other than the authentication TLV. Otherwise a hostile system could take an LSP, set Remaining Lifetime to zero and flood it to start a purge without knowing the password.

The memo also describes a password rollover issue. If the IS-IS process restarts right after rollover, its LSP Sequence Number restarts at 1 and neighbours reject the new LSPs. The router cannot raise its number because it cannot authenticate its own old LSPs. A suggested fix is to raise the number when an inbound LSP with the local System ID fails authentication but has a higher Sequence Number, with a counter to limit abuse by an active attacker.
sections.eli5: Routers can start by adding stamps without checking them, and can accept more than one secret while the secret changes. Messages that tell everyone to forget a route must be stamped too, or a troublemaker could erase real routes.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The memo says routing data does not need to be secret, but it should be authenticated so an adversary cannot inject false information. The mechanism is not perfect and does not need to be: it significantly raises the work an attacker must do without much implementation or operational complexity.

It does not prevent replay attacks, though in most cases existing IS-IS mechanisms would reject old information. Denial of service attacks are not generally preventable in a useful networking protocol.

The authors considered adding a Key-ID field, as OSPFv2 and RIPv2 have, but rejected it. The mechanism was already widely implemented in 1999 and widely deployed among interested users, and the improvement did not justify a change. Full digital signatures would be stronger but were rejected because of their computational burden.
sections.eli5: The stamp makes forging much harder but does not stop someone from replaying an old, real message. The authors chose a simple design that people already used.
